title: AI Hallucinations in State Farm Insurance Outside Lawyers' Filings

reading.body:
This is a case of a model asserting fabricated information as fact in a professional legal context. An AI tool generated nonexistent case citations, incorrect case titles, and invented quotations, and those outputs were submitted directly to a court across multiple filings without verification. The failure occurred at the point of human review, or rather the absence of it: the attorney believed the tool was connected to a verified legal research subscription and would check its own citations, an assumption that turned out to be wrong.

The failure mode is AI hallucination combined with deployment outside the conditions the tool was apparently built or vetted for, used as a substitute for independent citation verification rather than as an aid to it. Catching it would have required a lawyer to look up each cited case before filing, the standard manual check that the tool was incorrectly assumed to perform. The lead trial counsel accepted responsibility for the filings, and one attorney named the specific tool, Irys, as what she used.

What is not established is whether the tool itself was defective by design, whether the firm's subscription service made any representations about citation accuracy, or what consequences the court will impose.

reports.title: State Farm defense lawyers admit AI generated fake cases in LA lawsuit
AI hallucinated case law in insurance company’s filings in L.A. County house fire dispute
AI Hallucinations in State Farm Insurance Outside Lawyers' Filings

summary:
# Summary

State Farm's defense lawyers apologized for submitting court filings containing artificial intelligence-generated fabricated legal cases, fake quotes, and nonexistent legal holdings in a Los Angeles lawsuit. The case involves Fa'alagilagi Meni-Siliga, who sued State Farm after a 2020 fire destroyed her Carson home. She claimed the insurance company delayed approving repairs, and when a storm caused additional water damage during reconstruction, the work was never completed. Meni-Siliga stated that she and her husband exhausted their savings, retirement accounts, and eventually lost their home to foreclosure.

Lawyer Jacquelene Robinson admitted using an AI tool called Irys to prepare motions, mistakenly believing it was connected to her firm's legal research subscription and would verify citations. She confirmed that seven case citations across eight filings did not exist, along with incorrect case titles and fabricated quotes. Kenneth Katel, the lead trial counsel, accepted responsibility for the filings. The case is scheduled to go to trial in October. This incident reflects a growing trend, as 41 percent of law firms now use generative AI, though a database documents nearly 1,900 documented legal hallucination cases worldwide.
